canonical_statement: The study examined heparin kinetics in patients with thromboembolic disease and evaluated relationships between patient variables, kinetic parameters, and heparin dosage requirements.
The study included 20 patients with active thromboembolic disease: 12 men and 8 women, aged 18 to 86 years.
Thirteen patients had pulmonary emboli confirmed by lung scan and seven had deep-vein thrombosis confirmed by venography.

population.label: Patients with pulmonary embolism or deep-vein thrombosis

canonical_statement: The delay from symptom onset to initiation of heparin treatment ranged from 4 to 120 hours, with a median of 24 hours.
All 20 patients had normal renal function; 19 had normal liver function tests and one patient had abnormal liver tests that normalized 2 days after heparin was started.
Pretreatment heparin sensitivity was measured by adding beef lung heparin to plasma aliquots to produce concentrations of 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1 U/mL and measuring APTT in each aliquot.

exposures.details: Added in vitro to pretreatment plasma

canonical_statement: The APTT assay was run in duplicate with daily control validation; the normal pooled plasma control mean was 36 seconds with SD 1 second and coefficient of variation under 3%.
Each patient's heparin-sensitivity curve was estimated by linear least-squares regression of log change in APTT against log change in heparin concentration.
After pretreatment sensitivity testing, patients received an intravenous beef lung heparin bolus of approximately 70 U/kg.
APTTs were measured 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, and 2.5 hours after the heparin bolus, then converted to corresponding heparin concentrations using each patient's sensitivity curve.

outcome.definition: Derived from post-bolus APTT using the individual sensitivity curve

canonical_statement: Post-bolus concentration-time data were fitted by nonlinear least-squares regression to a single exponential term assuming a one-compartment model, yielding elimination rate constant, half-life, and peak heparin concentration.
Distribution volume was calculated as bolus dose divided by estimated peak heparin concentration, and clearance was calculated as elimination rate constant multiplied by distribution volume.

Maintenance infusion doses were individualized to target an APTT 1.5 to 2.5 times baseline: the desired steady-state heparin concentration came from the sensitivity curve and dose was calculated as clearance times desired concentration, rounded to the nearest 50 U/hour.

Determining sensitivity, collecting post-bolus samples, calculating the dose, and starting the individualized infusion required 3 to 4 hours; follow-up APTTs were obtained 6 to 12 hours after infusion initiation.

The analysis used Pearson correlations for variable pairs and forward stepwise multiple regression to model elimination rate constant, clearance, and dosage requirements; statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.
Pretreatment heparin-sensitivity curves showed approximately a 500% range across patients.
At a heparin concentration of 0.4 U/mL, the observed change in APTT ranged from 11 to 57 seconds across the 20 patients.
For every patient, the correlation coefficient between fitted and measured pretreatment APTTs was at least 0.93.

concept.text: Agreement of fitted and measured pretreatment APTT

canonical_statement: The slope of the heparin-sensitivity relationship correlated directly with baseline APTT (r = 0.46; p < 0.05).
Hematocrit was described as inversely correlated with baseline APTT (reported r = 0.43; p < 0.05), while heparin-sensitivity slope and hematocrit were not related.
Pretreatment heparin sensitivity did not differ significantly by sex or thromboembolic disease type, and it was not correlated with smoking or treatment delay.

Mean residuals between measured and fitted heparin concentrations were within approximately -0.01 to +0.01 U/mL across post-bolus intervals, supporting minimal apparent bias for the one-compartment fit.
Across all patients, mean heparin half-life was 0.88 hours (SD 0.29), with an observed range of 0.4 to 1.6 hours.
Across all patients, mean heparin elimination rate constant was 0.87 hr^-1 (SD 0.31), with an observed range of 0.44 to 1.72 hr^-1.
Smokers had a shorter mean heparin half-life than nonsmokers: 0.62 versus 0.97 hours (p < 0.05).
Smokers had a higher mean heparin elimination rate constant than nonsmokers: 1.19 versus 0.77 hr^-1 (p < 0.005).
A multiple regression model using sex, thromboembolic disease type, age, and smoking explained 63% of the variance in heparin elimination rate constant (p < 0.01).
The reported elimination-rate regression equation was Kd (hr^-1) = -0.123 Sex - 0.247 DVT - 0.005 Age (yr) + 0.387 Smoke + 0.906, with sex, smoking, and disease coded as dichotomous variables.
Mean heparin distribution volume was 3.27 L (SD 1.9) and ranged from 1.53 to 10.37 L.
Heparin distribution volume correlated with lean body weight (r = 0.60; p < 0.01).
Raw heparin distribution volume correlated with whole body weight (r = 0.55; p < 0.01).
Hematocrit did not correlate significantly with heparin distribution volume whether volume was expressed as liters, liters per kilogram, or liters per lean body weight.
Mean heparin clearance was 2.75 L/hour (SD 1.52) and ranged from 1.2 to 7.36 L/hour.
Men had a higher mean heparin clearance than women: 3.36 versus 1.83 L/hour (p < 0.05).
Heparin clearance correlated with lean body weight (r = 0.76; p < 0.001).
Heparin clearance correlated with whole body weight (r = 0.43; p < 0.05).
A multiple regression model using lean body weight, sex, and smoking predicted heparin clearance with multiple R = 0.78 (p < 0.005).
After lean body weight entered the clearance regression model, sex and smoking were no longer related to clearance and did not add predictive information.
Individualized heparin maintenance doses ranged from 500 to 2,000 U/hour; normalized to whole body weight, the mean requirement was 13.9 U/kg/hour (SD 3.6) with a range of 8.6 to 19.8 U/kg/hour.
Heparin dosage requirement correlated with lean body weight (r = 0.65; p < 0.001).
Heparin dosage requirement correlated with whole body weight (r = 0.76; p < 0.001).
Men required a higher mean whole-body-weight-normalized heparin dose than women: 15.3 versus 11.8 U/kg/hour (p < 0.05).
Patients treated within 24 hours of symptom onset (n = 9) required larger heparin doses than those whose treatment was delayed at least 24 hours (n = 11) (t = 2.37, df = 18, p < 0.05).

concept.text: Treatment within 24 hours of symptom onset

canonical_statement: A multiple regression model using whole body weight, sex, time from symptom onset to treatment, and smoking explained 78% of the variance in heparin dosage requirements (p < 0.001).
Follow-up APTTs ranged from 1.3 to 2.3 times baseline, with a mean of 1.7 times baseline; the mean desired APTT was 1.9 times baseline.
Heparin treatment lasted 2 to 16 days, and the number of dose adjustments of approximately 100 U/hour needed to maintain therapeutic APTTs ranged from zero to four.
Seven of 20 patients maintained therapeutic APTTs for the entire treatment course without any dose adjustment.
The mean and median time from heparin initiation to the first required dose adjustment were both 4 days.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: mean time to first dose adjustment

canonical_statement: No patient experienced bleeding during the reported heparin treatment course.
No patient experienced recurrent thromboembolism during the reported heparin treatment course.
One patient developed heparin-associated thrombocytopenia, and heparin was discontinued after 2 days of treatment.
The authors concluded that the kinetic individualization method was time consuming and expensive and was not yet recommended for clinical use.
The authors suggested that symptom timing, body weight, sex, and smoking history may be important factors when determining initial heparin dosage requirements.
The study was supported by the St. Paul-Ramsey Hospital Medical Education and Research Foundation, Grant 8178.
